content: Binocular vision refers to the ability to use both eyes together to perceive the environment. The term binocular is derived from the Latin words bin, meaning two, and oculus, meaning eye. Having two eyes provides several distinct advantages. Firstly, it offers a backup in case one eye is injured or impaired. Secondly, it expands the field of view; for instance, humans have a horizontal field of view of approximately 150 degrees with one eye, which increases to about 180 degrees when both eyes are used. Thirdly, binocular vision enhances the ability to detect faint objects through a process called binocular summation. Lastly, it enables stereopsis, which is the perception of depth created by the slightly different positions of the two eyes on the head. This depth perception is highly precise and is often accompanied by binocular fusion, where the brain combines the two images from each eye into a single coherent image. Other phenomena associated with binocular vision include eye dominance, utrocular discrimination, allelotropia, and binocular rivalry. In terms of field of view and eye movements, the positioning of the eyes varies among species based on their ecological needs. Prey animals, such as many birds, often have eyes on opposite sides of their heads, maximizing their field of view. Some birds can achieve a 360-degree field of view without moving their eyes. In contrast, predatory animals, such as cats, have forward-facing eyes that prioritize stereopsis over a wide field of view. These animals typically move their eyes together. Eye movements can be categorized as versions, where both eyes move in the same direction, or vergences, where the eyes move in opposite directions to focus on objects at varying distances. Convergence occurs when the eyes move inward to focus on a closer object, while divergence happens when the eyes move outward to focus on a more distant object. Some animals, like starlings, can employ both strategies, using lateral eye placement for a wide field of view and converging their eyes for stereopsis. Chameleons are particularly unique, as their eyes can move independently but also converge for depth perception when hunting. Binocular summation refers to the enhanced ability to detect stimuli when using both eyes compared to one. This occurs due to two mechanisms. The first is a statistical advantage, as having two detectors (eyes) increases the likelihood of detecting faint signals. This advantage is mathematically equivalent to the square root of two (approximately 1.41). The second mechanism involves neural summation, where certain cells in the visual cortex receive input from both eyes simultaneously, resulting in greater activity than the sum of the inputs from each eye individually. Binocular interaction encompasses several ways in which the two eyes influence each other. For example, light entering one eye affects the pupil size of both eyes, a phenomenon easily observed by alternately covering and uncovering one eye. Accommodation, or the focusing of the eye, is also linked between the two eyes. If one eye is closed and the other focuses on a nearby object, the closed eye will adjust its focus and converge as if it were open. This is due to a reflex that links accommodation and convergence. Additionally, interocular transfer occurs when the adaptation state of one eye slightly influences the other, such as when aftereffects induced in one eye can be perceived through the other. Utrocular discrimination is the ability to determine which eye received a monocular stimulus when both eyes are open. This ability is distinct from the fusion of images from both eyes. Singleness of vision, or binocular fusion, occurs when the brain combines the images from both eyes into a single image. This prevents confusion that could arise from the overlapping fields of view. If the brain fails to fuse the images, double vision (diplopia) occurs. Fusion is distinct from stereopsis, as fusion can occur even in the absence of depth perception. Fusion is limited to a specific volume of visual space around the fixation point, known as Panum's fusional area. Within this area, objects are seen as single, while outside of it, double vision occurs. The horizontal and vertical horopters define the boundaries of this area, with the horizontal horopter being a curved line through the fixation point and the vertical horopter tilted relative to the eyes. Eye dominance refers to the phenomenon where one eye's image takes precedence over the other when the brain cannot align the images from both eyes. This is particularly evident when pointing at a distant object. The dominant eye is the one whose image is prioritized. Stereopsis is the ability to perceive depth based on the parallax created by the different positions of the two eyes. There are two types of stereopsis: quantitative stereopsis, which provides accurate depth perception for objects within Panum's fusional area, and qualitative stereopsis, which allows for depth discrimination outside this area but without precise depth scaling. At extreme distances, depth perception diminishes, and the double images appear to lie on the fixation plane. Allelotropia occurs when the brain fuses the two monocular images of an object located off the horopter, resulting in a new visual direction. This direction is perceived as originating from a point between the two eyes, known as the cyclopean eye. The position of the cyclopean eye is typically closer to the dominant eye. Binocular rivalry arises when the two eyes are presented with significantly different images. In such cases, perception alternates between the two images, with one image being dominant for a few moments before switching to the other. This alternation continues as long as the conflicting images are presented. Disorders of binocular vision can occur when the eyes are not properly aligned. The six extraocular muscles control eye positioning, and slight differences in their strength, length, or insertion can lead to misalignment, especially when fatigued. This condition is known as phoria and can be revealed using the cover-uncover test. During this test, covering one eye disrupts the reflex that maintains proper alignment, and uncovering the eye reveals any misalignment. Exophoria occurs when the eye moves inward after being uncovered, while esophoria occurs when the eye moves outward. Vertical misalignments, such as hyperphoria and hypophoria, are less common. Cyclophorias, involving rotational misalignment, are even rarer. Persistent double vision (diplopia) following the test indicates a disorder. More severe misalignments, known as tropias, include exotropia (wall-eyed) and esotropia (cross-eyed), which are forms of strabismus often associated with amblyopia. Vertical tropias (hypertropia and hypotropia) and cyclotropias are also possible. In animals, binocular vision varies based on ecological needs. Predatory animals, such as cats, have forward-facing eyes with overlapping fields of vision to enhance depth perception. Herbivorous animals, such as horses, have laterally placed eyes with minimal overlap to maximize their field of view. This variation reflects the evolutionary adaptations of different species.
